sources.title: NGSS 5-ESS1-2: Represent data in graphical displays to reveal patterns of daily changes in length and direction of shadows, day and night, and the seasonal appearance of some stars in the night sky
NASA Night Sky Network: Spy the Scorpion (Scorpius in summer evenings)

steps.title: Sun
steps.instruction: Trace the sun in the middle.

note.text: This is a view from far above, looking down on the sun and Earth's path around it.

steps.title: Orbit
steps.instruction: Trace Earth's path around the sun.

note.text: Earth travels once around the sun every year.
note.remember: One trip around the sun = one year.

steps.title: Earth
steps.instruction: Trace Earth in winter and in summer.

note.text: Here is Earth at two times of year, half a year apart, as seen from the Northern Hemisphere.

steps.title: Looking out at night
steps.instruction: Draw the arrows pointing out from Earth's night sides.

note.text: At night we face away from the sun, so we see the stars on the far side of Earth from the sun.

steps.title: Orion
steps.instruction: Trace the seven stars of Orion.

note.text: Orion, the hunter, is a winter constellation. In winter, our night side faces toward it.
A constellation is a pattern of stars. The three in a row make Orion's belt.
Scorpius, the scorpion, shows up on summer evenings, when our night side faces the other way.

steps.title: Join Scorpius
steps.instruction: Connect the stars of the scorpion's curved body.

note.text: Its bright red star, Antares, is called the heart of the scorpion.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: Why can't we see Orion on summer nights?

options.text: In summer, Orion is on the sun's side of Earth, so it's up in the daytime
options.feedback: Yes. The stars are still there, but the bright sunlight hides them. We'd need to see stars in the daytime.
The stars stay put. Earth moves around the sun, changing which way our night side faces.
Stars shine all the time. In summer, Orion is in the daytime sky, hidden by sunlight.
It's not clouds. As Earth orbits, Orion ends up on the sun's side of the sky.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.question: When will Orion be back in the evening sky?

options.text: Next winter, when Earth returns to the same part of its orbit
options.feedback: Right. Earth's trip around the sun repeats every year, so the same constellations return each season.
It comes back every winter. Earth's yearly orbit makes the pattern repeat.
In summer, Orion stays hidden by daylight. It returns in the winter.
It's a yearly pattern: Orion returns every winter.
